content: Combivir is the trade name for a medication used in the treatment of HIV infection. It is a fixed-dose combination therapy that includes two antiretroviral agents: lamivudine, also known as 3TC and marketed under the brand name Epivir, and zidovudine, also referred to as AZT and sold under the brand name Retrovir. The combination of these two drugs provides a synergistic effect, meaning it is more effective in suppressing the virus than using either drug individually. Both lamivudine and zidovudine belong to a class of medications known as reverse transcriptase inhibitors. These drugs work by inhibiting the activity of reverse transcriptase, an enzyme that HIV relies on to replicate its genetic material and reproduce within the host's cells. By blocking this enzyme, Combivir reduces the amount of virus (viral load) present in the body and helps to increase the number of CD4 cells, which are critical components of the immune system. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Combivir for medical use on September 26, 1997. It was the thirteenth antiretroviral drug to receive FDA approval. Combivir is manufactured and marketed by the pharmaceutical company GlaxoSmithKline.
